# Phase 6 report (generated by `scripts/phase6_report.py`; do not edit by hand)

All timings: median of 3 repeats (1 repeat at x2/x4 -- see caveat below), single MacBook Air (10 CPU threads, 18 GB RAM), DuckDB memory capped at 11 GB, Spark local[10] with 10g driver memory. Same SQL text run on both engines (only the median function differs: DuckDB `median()`, Spark `percentile(x, 0.5)`) -- **result digests were compared and are byte-identical across engines at every size**, so the timing comparison is of equivalent work.

## Verdict, stated before the numbers so it can't be read as hype
**Spark was slower than DuckDB at every size tested, from 986K to 164.5M rows (up to 4.8 GB).** The gap narrows sharply as data grows past DuckDB's comfortable memory range (its process RSS approaches the 11 GB cap from ~41M rows on), but even at 164.5M rows / 4.8 GB, single-node DuckDB is still 3.5-11x faster than local Spark, not slower. This contradicts the common assumption that Spark 'becomes worth it' somewhere in the tens-of-millions-of-rows range on a single machine -- it did not, here, up to the largest size tested. The trend line suggests Spark *could* catch up at even larger scale (or with a real cluster instead of local[10] on a laptop), but that is a projection, not a measurement -- not claimed as fact. Spark's fixed ~4-6s JVM startup cost (`configure_spark_with_delta_pip`) also never amortizes below DuckDB's total time on these workloads.

**Caveat on x2/x4:** these are 1 run each (not median of 3) because of session time constraints, and the data is the real 41.1M rows *duplicated* 2x/4x (not 2x/4x independent real rows), so cardinality-sensitive operations (DISTINCT, GROUP BY) see artificially repeated keys. The relative engine comparison at a fixed size is still meaningful; the absolute row-count-to-time relationship past 41M rows should be treated as indicative, not precise.

## Delta storage: partitioning, compaction, Z-order (real 41,134,669-row table)
Same 3 queries (one code across hospitals; one hospital+type+10 codes; full-table top-5 aggregate) on 4 variants of the same rows via DuckDB's native Delta reader. V1 simulates ~13 months of daily incremental loads (400 small appends) to show what an unmaintained history table looks like.
| variant | files | median file size | size on disk | files overlapping the Q1 code range | Q1 (one code) | Q2 (hospital+codes) | Q3 (full agg) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| V0 real table (partitioned by hospital) | 52 | 103.3 MB | 4.42 GB | 52 | 0.037s | 0.015s | 0.184s |
| V1 fragmented (400 small appends, simulated) | 420 | 4.8 MB | 2.03 GB | 419 | 0.058s | 0.026s | 0.222s |
| V2 after OPTIMIZE (compaction) | 16 | 80.5 MB | 3.27 GB | 16 | 0.072s | 0.051s | 0.273s |
| V3 after Z-ORDER BY (code) | 8 | 133.6 MB | 4.31 GB | 1 | 0.015s | 0.027s | 0.146s |

OPTIMIZE (compaction) took 6.4s. Z-ORDER took 62.2s (rewrites and re-sorts every row, so it is not free -- run it on a schedule, not per-load).

**What each step actually bought:**
- **Compaction alone (V1->V2):** files 420->16 (less listing/open overhead), but the code-range-overlap column barely moved (419->16, i.e. still ~100% of files must be opened for a single-code query) because compaction does not sort the data -- point-query latency did not meaningfully improve.
- **Z-order (V2->V3):** file-pruning went from 16/16 files to **1/8** for the single-code query, and Q1 got faster than the original real table (0.015s vs the real table's 0.037s) -- because V0 was partitioned by hospital, not by code, so a single-code query there still touches every hospital's partition; Z-order by code prunes across hospitals instead.
- **Compaction without sorting is not enough for selective point queries; sorting (Z-order) is what actually enables file skipping.**

Note: V1-V3 use an 11-column subset (no SCD2 tracking columns) while V0 is the real 22-column history table, so **file-count and query-time comparisons are valid, the on-disk size comparison between V0 and V1-V3 is not apples-to-apples.**
